item.title: What a p-value Actually Tells You
item.description:
A p-value answers one narrow question: if the null hypothesis were true, how surprising is data this extreme or more extreme? It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it is not the probability that your result happened by chance.

A few things worth remembering when reporting or reading p-values:

  • Statistical significance is not practical significance. A tiny effect can be “significant” with a large enough sample.
  • p < 0.05 is a convention, not a law of nature. Treat it as one piece of evidence, not a verdict.
  • Report effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside p-values — the magnitude and uncertainty usually matter more than the threshold.

item.title: Time Series Forecasting: Where to Start
item.description:
Most time series methods, from ARIMA to gradient-boosted trees, are trying to separate a series into a few recurring pieces:

  1. Trend — the long-run direction.
  2. Seasonality — patterns that repeat at fixed intervals (weekly, yearly).
  3. Noise — what’s left after trend and seasonality are accounted for.

Once a series is decomposed this way, forecasting becomes a question of which piece is hardest to predict for your data — and that’s usually what determines whether a simple model (like exponential smoothing) will do, or whether you need something that can learn nonlinear structure (like an ML model with engineered lag features).

(Good place to link to one of your own papers — e.g. the lumpy skin disease or Omicron time series work — as a worked example.)

item.title: K-means Clustering, Without the Jargon
item.description:
K-means clustering groups data points by repeating two simple steps until nothing changes:

  1. Assign each point to its nearest cluster center.
  2. Update each cluster center to the average of the points assigned to it.

That’s the whole algorithm. The tricky parts in practice are usually:

  • Choosing k (the number of clusters) — the “elbow method” and silhouette scores are common starting points, but domain knowledge often matters more.
  • Scaling your features first — K-means uses distance, so a variable measured in the thousands will dominate one measured in decimals unless you standardize.
  • Initialization matters — K-means++ initialization avoids a lot of the bad-luck clustering that plain random starts can produce.

(This pairs well with a link to the socio-economic clustering paper on the Publications page.)
